newsitem.title: UK: Europe pager market seen poised to triple by 2001.
newsitem.headline: Europe pager market seen poised to triple by 2001.

text.p: The European paging market is poised to shake off its lethargy and triple to over 18 million subscribers by the year 2001, an independent telecoms management consultant said on Thursday.

Paris-based Eutelis, which published a report commissioned by key telecoms industry players, said the paging market in Europe had enormous growth potential but noted this was undervalued and under-supported both by telecoms operators and regulators.

European penetration of pagers, dubbed "the pauper's mobile telephone", stands at only around 1.5 percent. This compares to 15.8 percent in the U.S. and up to 30 percent in countries such as Singapore, Eutelis said.

But as manufacturers such as Philips Electronics NV promise to transform the traditionally inflexible, but low-cost, message receiver into a mini computer with micro keyboard which can also send messages and offer Internet access -- Europe is playing catch-up.

Some countries, such as France, are even expected to see their markets double this year as former "bleepers", formerly used by professionals such as doctors or plumbers, are re-positioned to appeal to the mass consumer market -- and the young.
"A pager is a device which could become as popular as a wrist watch," a spokesman for Eutelis told a news conference in London.

Bob Aerts, who conducted the study commissioned by industry heavyweights such as British Telecommunications Plc, France Telecom, Motorola Inc and Philips, said mass marketing and price-cuts would be key determining factors for greater market penetration.

"...the pager will offer major additional services, such as e-mail, message broadcasting, consultation of weather forecasts, news reports and even booking of travel arrangementsand data retrieving from bank accounts once two-way paging gets introduced," he added.
"The pager will no longer be the tool we know now, but a new device with many applications and differentiated services corresponding to the needs of increasing segmented user groups."

Eutelis echoed industry calls for regulators to allow paging operators to choose which technology they wanted to use and for new spectrum to be made available to enable anticipated growth -- both for the traditional one-way services and new two-way services.
